## Findings

### 1 — nit
- **Where:** app/Sources/CaptionRetime.swift:214
- **What:** `cutBack` reads the fixed neighbours from `before`. If an edit ever moved a non-re-timed caption, the cut-back would use its old place. `holds` would drop such a plan rather than corrupt anything.
- **Fix:** take the fixed neighbours' places from the post-edit snapshot (`now`), which the `still` guard already treats as the truth for re-timed captions.

### 2 — nit
- **Where:** app/Sources/CaptionRetime.swift:129-132
- **What:** The word times written relative to the snapped start can come out slightly negative when the start snaps later than the mapped time. `holds` (line 283) compares only the word count, so a `set_text` the core refused would leave stale word times unnoticed whenever no word was cut.
- **Fix:** clamp `relative` at 0, or have `holds` also compare the first word's start to the planned value.

# Screen recording and pause/resume (road map 3)

- **Status:** Built. R0 spike 2026-09-10 (q7 on 2026-09-12); R1 screen recording 2026-09-11 (`dd1d54f`); R2 pause/resume and the hidden panel 2026-09-12 (`54d71da` toll, `7a8fe31`). Reviewed and fixed. Issue batch B17 (2026-09-29): an unreadable segment is left out (#97); File ▸ Pause Recording and a fixed-width status item (#98 a, b). Issue batch B27 (2026-09-30): the countdown's mic meter (#98 c); a closed segment's late did-fail leaves that segment out (#181.1); a tool's status item flips at a pause or resume from any door (#181.4); `recording_proof.py`'s ffmpeg row names why ffmpeg will not run (#181.5). Include Frame Job windows (2026-09-30): the panel's checkbox and `record_screen`'s `include_framejob_windows`, off by default, put Frame Job's own windows in a display recording (spec §11 recording.md).
- **Original:** `archive/roadmap-3.md` (1586 lines) is the full record. Sections cited below as "orig §x" refer to it.
- **Spec decisions:** spec §11 has no IDs for these. They are the unnumbered bullets from "Screen recording is IN…" to "The recorder panel goes away…", and this document introduced all of them:
  screen IN, camera and callouts OUT · a recording is ordinary media · the file lives in `~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings/` · the canvas takes the recorder's rate and the media takes the file's · the panel asks for grants and the tool never does · microphone and system audio are two FILES · undo leaves the files on disk · a paused recording is a sequence of files over one stream · the panel goes away for every source. The same change also amended spec §1 (non-goal), §3, §7.4, §7.9, §9 (⌥⌘N) and the `async` bullet ("screen recording did not earn one").

## Context

Spec §1 made screen and camera recording non-goals on day one. Road map 2 §4 left capture as the user's call. Road map 3 took the screen half, because a screencast is the input the product was shaped around. Camera capture needs a second capture stack, and callouts need a metadata format plus an Input Monitoring grant, so both stayed out. The work added no op, no model field, no FFI export and no schema bump. It added one tool (`record_screen`), a recorder panel, a menu-bar status item and a landing path. R2 then added pause/resume, which ScreenCaptureKit does not provide, and moved the recording's controls into the menu bar at the user's request.

## Decisions

- **A recording is ordinary media, and the model learns nothing.** The file goes through File ▸ Open's own import path (`adoptImported`) or Add Media's two-try placement. There is no source kind, flag or schema change, so every op, cache and export already handles it. (orig §0 dec. 1; spec §11)
- **The file lives in `~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings/`, never in the package or the temp dir.** An untitled document has no package, and a recording is original footage, so it cannot go where caches are regenerable. Consolidate carries it in. `-RCRecordingFolder` overrides the location for proofs. Names follow the Screenshot app's spelling (`Screen Recording <date> at <h.m.s>.mov`), with ` (2)` added on a collision. (orig §0 dec. 2)
- **The canvas takes the recorder's rate (30/60), and the media record keeps the file's honest variable rate.** ScreenCaptureKit only sends a frame when the screen changes, so a probe measured 24981/1000 and 42381/1000. Without the override, that rate would become the timeline grid. `set_canvas` is not used afterwards because the untitled document's first project is not an undo step. (orig §0 dec. 3, R0 q4)
- **The panel asks for grants; `record_screen` never does.** The tool reads Screen Recording and Microphone status synchronously and refuses with the fix in the sentence. The microphone status is read BEFORE any `AVCaptureDeviceInput` exists, because that initializer prompts on its own. The panel asks unconditionally on a press. An early `canAsk` gate made a `notDetermined` microphone unrecoverable under `-AgentServerEnabled`. (orig §0 dec. 4, R1 record)
- **The refusal order is the caller's own mistakes first, then the grant, then the display/window lookup.** This keeps argument errors reachable on an ungranted machine, as `transcribe` does. The ordering rows in the proof kill a grant-first mutant. (orig R1d)
- **The microphone is a second `.m4a` file from `AVCaptureSession` + `AVCaptureAudioFileOutput`, never on the SCStream.** Measured: with `capturesAudio` and `captureMicrophone` both on, `SCRecordingOutput` writes ONE stereo track that is their SUM, which clipped at peak 1.218 in a smoke run. A cutter cannot separate them afterwards. The microphone lands on its own "Microphone" back track at the MEASURED per-segment did-start offset, never at a constant. (orig §0 dec. 5, R0 q2, q6b)
- **The capture session starts first, during the countdown (`prepareMicrophone`).** Starting inside `start` lost 421 ms of voice. With a prepared session the mic leads the picture by 65–75 ms, and the landing head-trims it. Session-first also gave the smaller offset, centred near zero; stream-first gave ~80 ms of picture with no mic. `session.startRunning()` blocks main for 100–180 ms, which is why it runs in the countdown. Since B27 the panel's meter reads that PREPARED session through the 3-2-1 (`publishMicrophoneLevel` while idle with a running prepared session; the tick armed at `beginCountdown`), and the discard publishes silence: the file output's connection was measured reporting levels on a running session before `startRecording` (2026-09-30, #98's comment — the real inputs moved with room noise; the virtual ones read a flat floor either way). (orig R0 q6b, R1 record; #98 c)
- **The picture uses `SCRecordingOutput`, with no `AVAssetWriter`.** `addRecordingOutput` goes BEFORE `startCapture`. Every call has a completion-handler form, so no `async` exception was needed. `recordingOutputDidStartRecording` arrives ~90–100 ms BEFORE `startCapture`'s completion, and the state machine tolerates that. (orig §2, R0 q2)
- **The composition holds a media's last frame when its video track ends early.** A screen recording's video track ends at the last screen change while audio runs on. AVFoundation renders the uncovered range BLACK (measured: picture at 1.5 s, black from 3 s). The fix is `CompositionBuilder.heldTail`, applied before speed scaling. The fix is in the composition, not the recorder, and a fully covered media is byte-identical. The filmstrip's held tail reads the track's last sample time through an `AVSampleCursor`, not the nominal rate. (orig "What R0 changes", R1 record)
- **`size: best` computes pixel dimensions itself.** `captureResolution` `.best` at point size gives a point-sized file. Pixels come only from `width`/`height` asked in pixels: the content filter's `contentRect` × `pointPixelScale` (R1; R0's spike read `CGDisplayCopyDisplayMode`), because `CGDisplayPixelsWide` reports points on Retina. H.264 rounds odd heights up. (orig R0 q4)
- **Show Clicks forces a BGRA pixel format.** `showMouseClicks` applies only under BGRA, and a fresh config is `420v`. `excludesCurrentProcessAudio` is ALWAYS true, so timeline playback stays out of the file. HEVC is used when offered, else H.264, and the container is `.mov`. (orig R0 q6a, R1a)
- **The programmatic filter excludes Frame Job by default** (`excludingApplications`). It removes 99.19 % of an excluded app's pixels. Whether a PICKER-made filter honours `excludedBundleIDs` for capture was never measured. It has been moot since R2 hides the panel for every source. Since 2026-09-30 the Include Frame Job windows checkbox (and `record_screen`'s `include_framejob_windows`) lifts it: no application is excluded, and a recording the panel started excludes the panel's own window (`excludingWindows`), which is on screen until `recordingDidStart`; the picker then lists Frame Job's windows but not the panel. `RecordingExclusion` is the one decision both doors and the picker read. (orig R0 q3; spec §11 recording.md, Include Frame Job windows)
- **`RecordingLanding` answers ops and predicted ids, and each door commits through its own path.** The panel uses `document.performGroupedEdit`. The tool uses `AgentServer.performGroupedEdit` / `editResult`, so a tool refusal never becomes a sheet. The ops come back unscoped and the door stamps the scope. (orig "What R0 changes")
- **The destination is `.document(recipeKey:)`, not `ObjectIdentifier`.** Object identifiers are reused at the same address after a close. A `recipeKey` is never minted twice, so a closed target falls back to `.newProject` exactly. (orig "What R0 changes")
- **The new-project order is a contract.** `openUntitledDocumentAndDisplay(false)` → `adoptImported` (first segment) → the import change-count → the remainder's one edit → `makeWindowControllers` → `showWindows`. Without the explicit import count, one ⌘Z left a new recording clean and ⌘W closed it without a prompt. (orig R1 record, R2b)
- **One grouped edit for all segments and mics ("one list, one limit").** A refused microphone pair takes the pictures down with it, and the files are named in the refusal. Landing half a recording with no undo step saying so was judged worse. A file the core cannot make any clip of lands as media with a note instead. (orig R1 record; `RecordingLanding.swift` doc)
- **A paused recording is a sequence of files over one stream.** ScreenCaptureKit has no pause. A pause REMOVES the recording output (its file closes in 5–25 ms). A resume ADDS a new one to a new file (starts in 8–10 ms), and the stream captures at ~57 fps throughout. The mic writer stops and restarts per segment on its one session. Each segment is named by its own start time, carries its own offset, and lands as a touching clip. Nothing joins the files afterwards. (orig §0 dec. 6, R0 q7; spec §11)
- **Segments land back to back on ONE track, with each end READ BACK from the trial.** The two-try rule applies to the whole sequence: all segments go on the front track, or all on a new one, so a recording never reads as two. At an inexact canvas rate, an `add_clip` at the previous end snapped DOWN into a one-tick overlap and minted a cross dissolve. So the rule is "touching, or a sub-frame gap, never an overlap". A segment's mic is floored at the previous mic's end, with head-trim rather than late placement. (orig R2b, R2 record)
- **The result has no first-segment conveniences.** `RecordingResult` carries `segments` and has no `micDescriptor` or `micOffset`, so a reader built for one segment fails to compile rather than going silently wrong. `pauses` is a STORED count, because `segments.count − 1` read 0 for a recording paused once and then stopped. (orig R2a, R2 record)
- **The panel orders out when the recording starts, for every source, and returns only with a note.** The status item is the recording's chrome: Pause/Stop, then Resume/Stop while paused, the coral dot, and the pause glyph with a frozen time, at one fixed width measured from its widest title (9:59:59). Pause and Resume have NO key; since B17 File ▸ Pause Recording (Resume Recording while paused) is a second door, with no MCP mirror (spec §11 recording). ⌥⌘N reads Stop Recording while a recording runs. ⌘Q while recording cancels the quit and opens the item's menu rather than finishing silently. There is no global hotkey, because it would need its own grant. (orig §0 dec. 7, R2c, §4)
- **`record_screen` is an off-main app-state tool with no `scope`.** It waits through a semaphore with `onMain` hops. The start waits `ScreenRecorder.armCeiling + 5` (25 s), then the span, then `stopCeiling(segments:)`, which grows with the segment count; R1's single `seconds + 30` ceiling is gone. Its span is WALL CLOCK, so a person's pause shortens what an agent's call records, and the result says so. A named `project` that does not resolve is refused, not silently redirected to a new document. (orig R1d, R2d, R2 record)
- **A microphone problem never fails the recording.** It becomes `micProblem` on a success. A picture that will not probe was the whole recording's failure until B17 (#97): now that segment is LEFT OUT and named in the result's `unreadable` with the files it kept, and only a recording with no readable movie fails, naming every file. Since B27 (#181) a CLOSED segment whose recording output reports a did-FAIL after its stop is left out the same way, unprobed, with the writer's sentence as its reason; only the did-fail of the segment still recording is the recording's failure. A mic failure at a segment boundary (a did-finish the machine asked for) is that segment's `micProblem` only, never the session's `microphoneProblem`. (orig R1 record, R2a; spec §11 recording)
- **The microphone needs the hardened-runtime entitlement `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` plus the plist usage key.** A bare `swiftc` probe needs neither, so spike rows measure the framework, not the app. (orig R0 closing)

## What it built — where it lives now

- Session: `app/Sources/RecordingSetup.swift` (choice, files, the pure `RecordingConfiguration.make`, `RecordingGrant`), `RecordingResult.swift`, and `ScreenRecorder.swift` with `+Pause`, `+Delegates`, `+Microphone`, `+Finishing` and `+Content` (shareable content fetched off main).
- Landing: `app/Sources/RecordingLanding.swift`, `+Placing`, `+Microphone`, and `ProjectDocument+Recording.swift` (`untitled(around:)`). `adoptImported` lives in `ProjectDocument.swift`.
- Chrome: `app/Sources/RecorderPanelController.swift` with `+Rows`, `+Recording`, `+Pause`, `+Landing` and `+Picker`; `RecorderStatusItem.swift`; `AppDelegate+Recording.swift`; the File menu item in `AppDelegate+Menus.swift`; the quit guard in `AppDelegate.swift`; the welcome button in `WelcomeWindowController.swift`.
- Tool: `app/Sources/AgentServer+Recording.swift`, `+RecordingArguments`, `+RecordingResult`, `+RecordingChrome` (the tool's status item, B27), and the catalog entry in `AgentCatalog+Files.swift` (the R1 toll cut from `AgentCatalog.swift`).
- Composition: `CompositionBuilder.heldTail` in `app/Sources/CompositionBuilder.swift`. The sparse-track tail is in `MediaImporter.swift`, and `MediaImporter+Probe.swift` came from R1's mid-wave toll.
- Build: `project.yml` (`entitlements`, `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`). `app/FrameJob.entitlements` is generated and git-ignored.
- Proof: `tools/proof/recording_spike.py` (R0 q1–q7, re-runnable), `recording_probe.py` (a probe over all of `app/Sources`, with a faked session and its own granted tier), and `recording_proof.py` (MCP, headless plus granted tiers). `tools/proof/README.md` holds the terminal-grant launch note.

## Known limits

- **TCC attribution:** a shell-launched binary runs under the TERMINAL's grants (R0 q1). A proof's instance therefore never tests Frame Job.app's own grant. `open -a … --env … --args …` gives an instance responsible for itself. `open -a` activates an existing instance instead of launching a new one.
- **Host state is a proof input.** A locked console lists 0 shareable displays under a true preflight. A muted output reaches the tap unreliably. Another app's sound lands in the tap. A Bluetooth OUTPUT gives the system-audio tap digital silence. A Bluetooth INPUT makes the mic lag the picture (see #57). The proofs skip these by name.
- **A variable-rate recording in a new project gives an inexact canvas rate only via File ▸ Open**, not via the recorder. At such a rate, "touching" segments may have a sub-frame gap.
- **Stopping and pausing edge cases** (documented in `ScreenRecorder+Pause.swift`):
  - A pause within ~10 ms of a resume's add can close an unopened file. Since B17 that empty movie is left out and named, not the recording's failure.
  - A mic start then stop before its first sample gives −11805 with no file. Since B17 it is that segment's `micProblem` alone, not `microphoneProblem` for the whole session.
  - A mic writer poisoned by a device profile switch (AirPods on first use, `'pck?'` −11800) fails every later segment's mic file.
- **A label past 9:59:59 is wider than the status item's one length.** The item is sized for ten hours; a longer recording's title is wider than `itemLength` (unmeasured how the bar draws it).
- **The countdown's meter holds its last pre-roll level through the ~0.1–0.2 s of arming**: the recorder publishes nothing while `.arming`, and `ScreenRecorder.swift` (399) was not touched to meter there (B27).
- **`recordedDuration` on `SCRecordingOutput` is whole seconds.** It serves the timer only, never an offset.
- **Structural-only coverage:** four rules are read, not driven, by the probe — the tool's `try?` on a nil, `freeze()`, the quit guard's `openMenu()`, and the panel close in `.starting`.
- **Rejected or left out:** camera recording (a second capture stack; spec §1 non-goal); keystroke/click callouts (event tap plus Input Monitoring; only `showMouseClicks` is taken); a global stop hotkey (needs a grant); trimming the countdown or any post-processing; recording into the package; HDR (the pipeline is 8-bit BGRA); a `.microphone` stream output for the meter (it works, ~94 buffers/s in the device's native format, but it is moot). The meter polls `AVCaptureAudioChannel` levels at ~28 Hz from main instead, with no queue.

docs/guide/assistant.md:105:- import, relink and remove media, copy it into the project (it asks first), and set a media's camera log
docs/guide/audio.md:3:Frame Job mixes sound from every clip that has it: a camera clip, an audio-only file, a microphone recording or a nest. Each clip has its own level, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan and mono fold, and each track can be muted or soloed. Two commands do the measuring for you. Normalize sets a clip's level from its loudest moment, and Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by their sound. The preview and the export use the same mix, so what you hear while editing is what gets written.
docs/guide/audio.md:239:**Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** lines up two or more clips by their sound. The usual case is a camera clip and a separate audio recorder that captured the same moment. Select the clips, each on its own track, and choose the command. One clip, the **anchor**, stays where it is. Every other clip slides along its own track until its sound plays at the same moment as the anchor's.
docs/guide/audio.md:247:In other words, a camera clip stays put and the recorder moves to it.
docs/guide/audio.md:252:- **It searches the trimmed parts first.** Frame Job first looks for a match within the parts of each clip you have trimmed it to. It searches the whole files only if that finds nothing and one of the clips is trimmed. If a recording contains more than one similar stretch, trim the recorder roughly around the camera's sound so it matches the right one.
docs/guide/color-grading.md:34:The order the grade is applied in is fixed: Color first, then Light, Wheels, Curves (tone curves, then the hue curves) and the Look. The clip's filters from the Picture tab's **Filters** section split around the grade: Pixelate, Blur and Sharpen act on the picture before it, and Sepia, Noir, Vignette and Invert act after the Look, in the order of their slots. That matters when you combine a filter such as Noir or Vignette with a grade. A camera-log conversion set on the media comes before all of them (see [HDR and colour management](hdr-and-color.md)).
docs/guide/color-grading.md:179:- "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice." A creative LUT is fine there; a camera LUT would convert the footage a second time.
docs/guide/color-grading.md:182:See [HDR and colour management](hdr-and-color.md) for camera log and HLG projects.
docs/guide/color-grading.md:184:**Removing a LUT.** A LUT counts as used by every clip whose look it is, and by every file whose Camera Log it is. Removing it from the Media tab asks first, naming those uses, and its **Remove and Clear Looks** button removes the LUT and clears the look from those clips (they keep their place) and the Camera Log from those files. An action whose end names the removed LUT simply stops changing the look.
docs/guide/color-grading.md:275:Some things are not part of the grade, so Show Ungraded leaves them on: a camera-log conversion on the media, filters, the chroma key, and placement. Exports, **Save Frame…** and the look gallery's thumbnails never see the switch.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:3:Frame Job reads each source as what it is: iPhone HDR video, HDR10 files, wide-gamut footage and camera log. It converts each one into the project's working colour before any grade, key or blend touches it. A project works in **SDR** (Rec. 709, the default) or in **HDR (HLG)** (Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020). An HDR project exports an HLG master, an HDR10 file or an SDR version, and you can preview that SDR version at any time. This page covers telling Frame Job how a file was shot, choosing the project's dynamic range and its blending, and the depth and colour you get in exports and saved frames.

docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:20:The conversion is Frame Job's own. It works the same way in the preview, in every export, in rendered and saved frames, and in the timeline's filmstrip and the Media tab's thumbnails. Changing a file's Camera Log redraws its thumbnails. An HLG or PQ still's thumbnail appears once its converted tile is ready, a moment after import.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:24:## Camera log
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:26:Log footage looks flat and grey until it is converted. The **Camera Log** section of the **Media** tab tells Frame Job which curve a video file was shot with. The section appears once the project has a video file.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:31:It is a setting on the *file*, so every clip of that file follows it, reversed clips included. It is one undo step, **Camera Log**. A line under the popup says what is set. It reads "Select a video in the list" when the selected row is not a video file, and the popup is disabled. The section's header shows the selected file's setting (its curve or LUT name), so you can read it with the section collapsed.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:33:Relinking a file (**Relink…**) keeps its Camera Log setting.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:37:| Item | Curve | Camera gamut |
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:62:**Use LUT…** opens a file panel asking you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709." The LUT is added to the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all in one **Camera Log** step. Its output is taken as Rec. 709. Other files can then pick it from the popup as **LUT: *name***. If that LUT is already in the Media list, its entry is reused instead of a second one being added. A file that can't be read as a LUT shows an error.
docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md:64:A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used: **Unused only** hides it, and Remove asks first.

questions.question: What should a camera recording capture?

options.label: Camera, or camera + screen (Recommended)
options.description: Camera on its own, OR at the same time as a screen recording (a talking head over a screencast). Each lands as its own file and track, the camera above the screen, placed as a corner picture-in-picture you can move.

options.label: Camera alone
options.description: A camera feed only, like Photo Booth or QuickTime's Movie Recording. Simpler; camera + screen can come later.

options.label: Camera + screen only
options.description: Only as an overlay on a screen recording, never on its own.

questions.question: Where should you start a camera recording?

options.label: The existing recorder panel (Recommended)
options.description: The panel gains a Camera source (and a camera row when recording the screen): one panel, one countdown, one menu-bar status item with Pause/Stop, the same landing into the project. File ▸ New Recording (⌥⌘N) stays the one door.

options.label: A separate command
options.description: File ▸ New Camera Recording with its own panel and live preview, separate from screen recording.

questions.question: Which cameras, and what should the panel show?

options.label: Built-in and USB cameras
options.description: The Mac's FaceTime camera and any USB/UVC webcam or capture card macOS lists.

options.label: iPhone Continuity Camera
options.description: Your iPhone 18 Pro as a wireless camera, through macOS's Continuity Camera.

options.label: Live preview in the panel
options.description: A small live picture of the chosen camera in the panel before you record, so you can frame yourself.

options.label: Resolution and frame-rate choice
options.description: A popup for the camera's formats (e.g. 1080p30, 4K30, 720p60); otherwise the camera's best format is used.

questions.question: Where does the sound come from when recording a camera?

options.label: The chosen microphone, own file (Recommended)
options.description: As screen recording does today: the microphone you pick (which can be the camera's own mic) is a separate audio file on its own track, lined up to the picture. Keeps it separately editable.

options.label: Embedded in the camera file
options.description: The microphone's sound is written into the camera's movie file as one clip with picture and sound.

There's an open source auto-updating library. What is it?

It's **Sparkle** (sparkle-project.org, github.com/sparkle-project/Sparkle), the standard open-source auto-updater for macOS apps distributed outside the Mac App Store.

- **How it works:** the app checks an **appcast**, an RSS-style XML feed listing versions, on a schedule or from a "Check for Updates…" menu item. When there's a newer version it shows release notes, downloads the update, verifies it and installs it.
- **Security:** every update is signed with an **EdDSA (ed25519)** key. Sparkle verifies that signature as well as Apple's code signature, so a compromised download host can't push a fake update.
- **Distribution:** it accepts the DMG or zip you already publish. The appcast can live on GitHub Releases or GitHub Pages, so there's no server to run.
- **Fit with Frame Job:**
  - The `publish` workflow already produces Developer ID-signed, notarized DMGs on GitHub Releases. Adding Sparkle would mean signing each DMG with the EdDSA key and updating the appcast in that same workflow.
  - The app side is a Swift package and a menu item.
  - Sparkle 2 also supports sandboxed apps, through its XPC services.

If you want it, I can start it as a road map like the camera one. It would need two things from you: the EdDSA private key stored as a GitHub Actions secret, which only you can create, and a choice of where the appcast lives.
Let's do it. Use /litecode

# Frame Job

A native macOS video editor. Open a movie, arrange it on layered tracks over a
fixed canvas, then trim, cut, grade, caption, animate and export it. Every edit
you make in the window can also be made by an AI agent over MCP, or by the
built-in Assistant, and each one is an ordinary undo step.

Apple Silicon, macOS 26 or later. There is no account to make: every
AI feature runs on your own API key (Anthropic for the Assistant, AssemblyAI
for cloud transcription), and everything else works without one.

## Open a movie and start cutting

**File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) on a `.mov` or `.mp4` — or a drop on the Dock icon, or
**Open Video…** in the Welcome window — creates an *untitled* project sized and
rated to that file, with the file as the first clip on Track 1, ready to cut. A
portrait phone clip opens portrait, and a 29.97 fps file stays 29.97. **Save**
then writes a `.framejob` package, offered next to the source.

## Features

**Projects and media.** Movies, sound and pictures from everything macOS plays,
plus WebM and MKV copied in without re-encoding; missing files relinked;
Consolidate Media copies footage into the package.
→ [Projects and media](docs/guide/projects-and-media.md)

**Timeline.** One kind of track that holds any clip; a frame-accurate ruler,
filmstrips and waveforms, zoom about the cursor, snapping, markers, an in/out
range, track mute, solo and lock, clip names and colour labels.
→ [The timeline and playback](docs/guide/timeline.md)

**Editing.** Move, nudge, trim, slip, roll, split, lift, ripple delete, close
gap, insert time, insert and overwrite, copy and paste, Paste Attributes, and
nests that group clips into one.
→ [Editing clips](docs/guide/editing.md)

**Canvas and layers.** Move, scale, rotate and crop on the preview; opacity,
blend modes, shadows, filters, chroma key, spotlight and obscure; text, shape,
image and background clips; matte tracks that cut the track behind them.
→ [Canvas, layers, text and shapes](docs/guide/canvas-and-layers.md)

**Motion and transitions.** Actions that ease any property to a new state over
a span — Zoom to Region for screencasts — motion presets for entrances, exits
and continuous movement, and thirteen transition styles.
→ [Motion, actions and transitions](docs/guide/motion-and-transitions.md)

**Speed.** Constant speed or fit to a length, ⌥-drag rate stretch, keep pitch,
reverse, freeze frame, and speed ramps — **Clip ▸ Speed Ramp…** makes a Ramp
Up, Ramp Down, Speed Dip or Speed Burst in one step.
→ [Speed, reverse and freeze frames](docs/guide/speed.md)

**Audio.** Per-clip volume, fades, ducking, noise reduction, compressor, pan and
mono; Normalize; Synchronize Audio lines up a camera and a separate recorder by
their sound, drift included.
→ [Audio](docs/guide/audio.md)

**Clean-up tools.** Remove Silences cuts dead air by voice or by level; Remove
Filler Words cuts the ums and uhs on their own timings. Both preview the cuts
and make them as one undo step.
→ [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md)

**Captions.** Import SubRip, export SubRip or WebVTT; generate captions on this Mac
or with AssemblyAI, as two-line subtitles or word-by-word captions in five
styles. Every caption is an ordinary text clip.
→ [Captions and transcription](docs/guide/captions.md)

**Colour grading.** Light and colour controls, three wheels, curves, eight
built-in looks and your own `.cube` LUTs, adjustment clips with qualifiers,
Show Ungraded, and waveform, parade, vectorscope and histogram scopes.
→ [Colour grading](docs/guide/color-grading.md)

**HDR and colour management.** iPhone HDR, HDR10, wide gamut and camera log
read as what they are; SDR or HDR (HLG) projects; HLG, HDR10 and SDR-version
deliverables, with Show SDR Version to preview the last.
→ [HDR and colour management](docs/guide/hdr-and-color.md)

**Motion graphics.** Graphic clips drawn every frame by a small JavaScript
module: six built-ins (Bar Chart, Callout, Counter, Kinetic Type, Lower Third,
Title Card), properties as inspector controls, your own modules too.
→ [Motion graphics](docs/guide/graphics.md)

**Screen recording.** A display or a window, with system audio, microphone and
click rings, at 30 or 60 fps, into a new project or at the playhead; a camera,
on its own or beside the screen as a corner talking head; or a
microphone-only voice-over.

**Export.** H.264, HEVC (8-bit, 10-bit, with alpha), ProRes 422 and 4444,
M4A, WAV, AIFF, GIF and animated PNG; loudness targets, presets, an Export
Queue that runs while you edit, and single frames as stills.

Also: [Settings](docs/guide/settings.md) and
[Menus and keyboard shortcuts](docs/guide/menus-and-shortcuts.md).

## Getting Frame Job

The newest signed and notarized build is always at
<https://github.com/kpgalligan/framejob/releases/latest/download/FrameJob.dmg>.
While the repository is private, the link works only for people with access to
it. Open the DMG and drag Frame Job to Applications. An installed copy
updates itself (Frame Job ▸ Check for Updates…, [Settings](docs/guide/settings.md#updates)).

To build it yourself, see [Developing Frame Job](docs/developing.md).

## Using it with an AI agent

Frame Job serves its editor as MCP tools on a local socket only programs you
run can open. An MCP client reaches it through `framejob-mcp`, a helper inside
the app, which starts Frame Job in the background on the first tool call if it
is not running. **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ MCP ▸ Copy MCP Command** puts the
Claude Code registration line on the clipboard, with your copy's path:

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user framejob -- '/Applications/Frame Job.app/Contents/Helpers/framejob-mcp'
```

[MCP](docs/guide/mcp.md) covers other clients and every tool;
[the Assistant](docs/guide/assistant.md) is the same tools inside the window.

## Documentation

- [The user guide](docs/guide/README.md) — every feature, by task.
- [The graphics API](docs/graphics-api.md) — writing a graphic module.
- [Manual checks](docs/manual-checks.md) — what only a person at the machine
  can confirm, run before each release.
- [The spec](designs/spec/README.md) — the normative design, one file per
  section.
- [Developing Frame Job](docs/developing.md) — building, testing, the
  architecture and publishing a release.

## Building

Xcode 26, Rust, xcodegen and bun; then `make app`. Everything else is in
[docs/developing.md](docs/developing.md).

content.text:
I built a 91.5-second promo, 1920×1080 at 30 fps, in the open project. It's saved as `~/Movies/Frame Job Promo.framejob` and exported to `~/Movies/Frame Job Promo.mp4` (H.264, 25 MB). The export reported no graphic warnings, and I checked frames pulled from the finished file.

The project had no footage, so every scene is a graphic module in Frame Job's brand colours (cream, green, yellow, coral), drawn as stylised illustrations rather than screenshots of the app.

| # | Scene | Length |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Intro: the logo assembles, then "A native video editor for macOS" | 5 s |
| 2 | Editing: a mock timeline where a playhead sweeps, a clip is cut out and the gap closes | 8 s |
| 3 | **Motion graphics:** a JS module types itself out, its preview springs to life, and inspector controls restyle it | 11 s |
| 4 | **The six built-in graphics**, each animating in its own card | 8 s |
| 5 | **Actions:** a dial whose value, colour and spin are animated by a real action on the timeline | 7 s |
| 6 | **Matte tracks:** a moving colour field seen through "MOTION" letters | 6 s |
| 7 | Colour grading: ungraded vs graded split, wheels and a waveform | 7 s |
| 8 | Captions: a real word-by-word caption with a gliding highlight | 6 s |
| 9 | Remove Silences / Filler Words: the gaps and "um"s close up | 7 s |
| 10 | Screen and camera recording | 5.5 s |
| 11 | Export formats and the Export Queue | 5 s |
| 12 | Agents: a mock Claude Code session calling the MCP tools, the Assistant tab, and "This video was made by Claude, over Frame Job's MCP tools." | 9 s |
| 13 | Outro: logo, tagline, `github.com/kpgalligan/framejob` | 7 s |

- **The motion-graphics section uses the real features.** The dial in scene 5 is moved by an action set on its clip, not by its own code. The matte scene is a true alpha matte track over a separate graphic track. The caption is an ordinary text clip with word timings and a highlight style.
- **Transitions:** there is one between every pair of scenes, using push, zoom, wipe, dissolve and slide, with a dip to black before the outro.
- **Timeline layout:** there are four tracks: Scenes, Fill, Matte (alpha) and Overlay.
- **Editing text:** every headline and bullet list is a module property, so you can reword it in the inspector without touching code.

Before you use it:
- **There's no audio.** You'll want a music bed.
- **The GitHub URL on the end card** only works once the repo is public, which hasn't happened yet.
- **The agent scene is illustrative.** The tool calls shown are a representative sample, not a log of this session, and the Assistant's reply and its "$0.04" cost are made up.
- **The project was untitled,** so I saved it to `~/Movies` to keep the graphics with it. Move or rename it as you like.
Any music suggestions?

For this cut I'd go with **upbeat electronic or indie-tech at about 115–125 BPM**: a clean pulse, a light synth or plucked-guitar hook, and no vocals so the on-screen text carries the story. The scenes are flat, colourful and change every 5–11 seconds, which suits something driving but not aggressive. Avoid epic or cinematic tracks, which would swamp the playful graphics.

**Shape to look for**
- **0–5 s:** a soft intro under the logo build.
- **About 5 s:** the beat drops as the editing scene pushes in.
- **24–29 s:** a lift or build through the motion-graphics stretch (code → built-ins → actions → matte), which is the part you want to feel biggest.
- **About 76 s:** a breakdown or half-time feel under the agent scene, so "This video was made by Claude" lands.
- **84–91 s:** a resolving outro under the end card.

A track of about 90 seconds, or a longer one with a clean ending to cut to, is ideal.

**Search terms:** "tech product launch", "upbeat corporate electronic", "future bass light", "indie electronic positive", "app promo".

**Where to look.** Check each site's current licence terms yourself; they change, and some require attribution.
- **Free:**
  - Pixabay Music, with a broad free-use licence.
  - Uppbeat, free with a credit line.
  - Free Music Archive, filtered to CC BY or CC0.
  - Incompetech (Kevin MacLeod, CC BY with attribution).
- **Paid, worth it if this becomes a real launch video:** Artlist, Epidemic Sound or Musicbed. These have cleaner licensing for anything published widely.
- **YouTube Audio Library** is fine if the video lives only on YouTube. Some of its tracks are restricted elsewhere.

**Once you've picked a track**, give me the file path and I can:
- import it and lay it under the whole cut, with a fade in and a fade-out timed to the logo;
- move the scene cuts onto its bars. At 120 BPM a bar is 2 s, so most scenes need only small trims;
- export with loudness normalised to −14 LUFS, the usual streaming target.

content.text:
Mostly yes. The steps are already in the frame Frame Job renders, before the H.264 encode touches it.

**What I measured** on the intro's green glow, along an 800 px line from the left edge to the logo:

| | Green levels used | Typical flat band | Widest band |
|---|---|---|---|
| `render_frame` output (before encoding) | 43 (values 23–65) | 14 px | 50 px |
| Exported H.264, same frame | 41 | 10 px | 56 px |

The glow only moves from #0D1512 to a mid green, so it spans about 40 code values per channel. Spread over 800 px, each value becomes a flat ring about 15–50 px wide. Every edge you see is a single-step change, which is exactly what 8-bit can't subdivide. Red, green and blue step at different radii, so the rings also pick up a faint colour tint.

**Why it's 8-bit.** Graphic clips are rasterized by resvg into 8-bit BGRA. That's a recorded decision (spec §11 PR-5: graphics, text and shapes stay 8-bit) even though the compositor itself works in 16-bit float. So a 10-bit export (HEVC 10-bit or ProRes) would not fix it: the steps are baked in before the compositor sees the graphic. The H.264 encode then adds a little on top, making bands slightly narrower and blockier, but it isn't the main cause.

**What would fix it**
1. **Add grain in the graphics (works today).** A faint noise layer over each gradient, using an SVG `feTurbulence` filter at about 3–5% opacity, breaks the hard band edges into texture even at 8-bit. It's the standard cure for banding in motion design. It does cost bitrate, so I'd also export at around 20–25 Mbps so H.264 keeps the grain instead of smoothing it back into bands. Only the intro, outro and colour-field scenes have large soft gradients.
2. **Make the gradient span less dark range.** A smaller, brighter glow uses fewer, more spread-out steps in a range where the eye notices them less. This is a design compromise, not a real fix.
3. **Fix it in the product.** Graphics would need either a deeper raster or dithering when the gradient is drawn. Either one goes against the PR-5 decision, so it's your call. I can file an issue for it.

content.text:
Yes, but expanding the SVG depth alone won't remove the banding from most videos. There are two 8-bit steps, and the second applies to every H.264 export.

**1. The graphic raster is 8-bit.** Graphics are drawn by resvg on top of tiny-skia 0.12, and tiny-skia only has an RGBA8 pixel buffer. It already computes gradients in 32-bit float internally, then rounds to 8 bits when it writes the pixel. To keep that precision we would have to:
- patch tiny-skia, vendored, to write 16-bit pixels;
- force every graphic through its float pipeline. Today simple fills take a faster 8-bit path, so drawing a graphic would get slower; a spike would measure by how much;
- accept that resvg's own filters (blur, `feTurbulence`) would stay 8-bit unless patched too.

On the app side the graphic texture becomes `rgba16Float`, which the compositor already uses. Each cached graphic frame doubles in memory, so the graphics cache (a quarter of RAM) holds half as many frames. This reopens spec §11 PR-5, which deliberately kept graphics 8-bit.

**2. The final 8-bit output has no dithering.** The compositor works in 16-bit float, but H.264 and 8-bit HEVC (the default and most common exports) round it to 8 bits, and I found no dither anywhere in the app or shaders. Even a perfect 16-bit gradient lands back in 8-bit steps at that point. The same is true of graded deep footage, such as a smooth sky. Only the 10-bit and ProRes exports would show the benefit of deeper graphics.

**What I'd build**
- **Deep graphics:** tiny-skia patched to write 16-bit, uploaded as `rgba16Float`. This fixes banding in 10-bit and ProRes deliverables and stops gradients losing levels when a graphic is graded, faded or scaled.
- **Dither at every 8-bit output:** a small deterministic noise, about half a level, added in the compositor when the target is 8-bit (H.264, HEVC 8-bit, PNG stills). This is what makes the bands disappear in an ordinary H.264 file, and it helps video as well as graphics.

The dither alone would fix most of what you're seeing for most deliverables, and it's the smaller change. Deep graphics without the dither would barely change an H.264 export.

**How I'd run it:** a short spike first, then the road map in a worktree lane, recording the new §11 decision (superseding PR-5 for graphics) before any code. The spike would answer three things on the intro gradient:
- how many levels the patched raster keeps;
- how much slower drawing and how much more memory it costs;
- whether the dithered H.264 export still shows bands at default bitrate.

Should I start with the spike?
Lets do dither now, and record the more involved changes for later.
I'll file the deep-graphics work as an issue first, then run the dither through litecode in its own worktree lane.

## What was measured (2026-10-27)

The promo's intro graphic draws a radial gradient from `#0D1512` to a mid green over ~800 px. Along row 540, x 0–800, of a 1920×1080 `render_frame` PNG:

- green spans code values 23–65: 43 distinct levels, 51 steps, every step exactly one level;
- median flat run 14 px, widest 50 px: visible concentric rings, faintly tinted because R, G and B step at different radii.

The same frame decoded from the H.264 export keeps 41 levels (median run 10 px, widest 56 px): the encode is not the main cause. The steps are in the raster.

## Why it is 8-bit

- `graphic/` renders through resvg 0.48.1 on tiny-skia 0.12.0. tiny-skia's only `Pixmap` is RGBA8.
- Its highp pipeline already evaluates gradients in f32, and rounds to u8 at the store stage. Its lowp pipeline (u16 fixed point) runs whenever every stage has a lowp form, as simple fills do. It has no dithering (a `// TODO` about `dither_rate` in `pipeline/blitter.rs`).
- resvg's filters (`feGaussianBlur`, `feTurbulence`, …) operate on 8-bit buffers.

## What expanding it would take

1. A vendored tiny-skia patch: a 16-bit (f16 or u16) `Pixmap`, a deep store stage for highp, and forcing highp for graphics. Raster time will rise; measure it.
2. resvg's filters: patch them to the deep buffer, or document that a filtered region stays 8-bit.

5. Proofs: graphics_proof and every frozen graphic baseline compare 8-bit pixels; they re-record or gain a deep comparison.

Payoff: banding-free graphics in the 10-bit and ProRes deliverables, and gradients that keep their levels when a graphic is graded, faded or scaled. For 8-bit exports the output dither (done separately) is what removes the bands, so do this after it.

result.output:
# Spec §11 — decisions: Foundations (M1–M3, road map 2)

Part of spec §11, *Decisions made — do not re-litigate*. The index of every decision is
[`README.md`](README.md).

- **AVFoundation, not ffmpeg.** Risk: MKV, WebM/VP9 and AV1-in-MKV do not
  open. Mitigation (M3, landed): an opt-in import step that shells out to a
  user-installed ffmpeg (present at `/opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg` on the
  development machine) to rewrap or transcode. The conversion is written to
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/Rewrapped/`, **not into the
  package**, for two reasons the `FFmpegRewrap.rewrapDirectory` comment
  spells out: opening an MKV from the Finder makes an UNTITLED document, so
  the import that needs a conversion is exactly the one with no package to
  put it in; and `fileWrapper(ofType:)` is a two-child whitelist whose one
  surviving location, `cache/`, is documented-regenerable (§5.6) — the last
  place for the only decodable copy of someone's footage. The name carries
  a digest of path, size and modification date, so a conversion is reused
  and invalidates itself. `RCFFmpegImport` chooses the policy and
  `RCFFmpegPath` the binary; with neither ffmpeg nor a cached conversion
  the import fails exactly as it did before the feature existed.
  Amended by #216-R: WebM and Matroska open by a built-in rewrap; ffmpeg
  remains the opt-in step for what that does not copy.
  Amended by #227: that step copies a constant-rate VP9 Profile 0 or 2
  video stream rather than re-encoding it, kept only when every frame of
  the copy is on its rate's grid.
  **Amended by NM-4** (rename R0):
  `~/Library/Application Support/Reelcut/Rewrapped/` is now
  `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/Rewrapped/`.
- **Custom compositor from day one** (M1 step 5). `AVVideoCompositing`
  has sharp edges — pixel-buffer pools, timing, `renderContextChanged`.
  Building the single-layer version first de-risks every later effect.
- **`AVPlayerLayer` under an overlay view**, not a self-driven `MTKView`,
  for the preview: A/V sync and scrubbing come from the player; the
  overlay maps through `videoRect`.
- **One JSON op entry point** (`rc_project_apply`) instead of one C
  function per op. Trade-off accepted: argument checking moves to
  Rust (`Err`) and to the typed Swift builders; in return the header is
  stable and the MCP catalog is the same table.
- **The plan-string compare** decides rebuild vs. refresh. Simple, and
  correct by construction because the plan contains exactly the

content.text:
Yes, but macOS can't do the encoding for us. Apple provides decoders for these formats on some Macs and no encoders on any, so Frame Job would need its own encoder.

**What I checked on this Mac (M2 Max, macOS 26.5.1)**
- **No AV1 or VP9 encoder exists in VideoToolbox.** The system's encoders are only H.264, HEVC (including alpha), ProRes, JPEG and H.263. That's true of every Mac: Apple's AV1 hardware on M3 and later decodes only.
- **No hardware decode here.** Neither AV1 nor VP9 reports hardware decode on this machine. That's the "depending on the machine" you've seen on import: AV1 only plays on M3 or later, and VP9 relies on macOS's own decoder.
- **AVFoundation can't write WebM at all.** VP9's usual home is WebM. AV1 normally goes in MP4.

**Ways to add it**

1. **Use ffmpeg, if the user has installed it.** This copies the import precedent in spec §11, where WebM/MKV conversion can shell out to an ffmpeg the user installed themselves. The export would feed frames to `ffmpeg` with SVT-AV1 or libvpx-vp9.
   - Cheapest by far.
   - The app stays free of ffmpeg.
   - It only works for people who have ffmpeg with those encoders installed.
2. **Bundle the encoders.**
   - **Libraries:** SVT-AV1 (BSD + AOM patent licence) and libvpx (BSD), both compatible with Apache-2.0, built into the app.
   - **Muxers:** AV1 needs an MP4 muxer; whether AVFoundation can carry AV1 samples is unverified, so this is a spike question. VP9 needs a WebM muxer, which would be new code. The core already reads Matroska but doesn't write it.
   - **Cost:** a real road map, plus build work for the C libraries.
   - **Alternative:** rav1e is a pure-Rust AV1 encoder, but it would break the architecture rule that Rust does no pixel work, so that would be your call.
3. **Either way, it's slow.** Encoding is software-only. SVT-AV1 at fast presets can roughly keep pace at 1080p; VP9 and high-quality AV1 are several times slower than real time. They'd suit the Export Queue, not quick previews.

**Is it worth it?** For uploads, not really: YouTube and most platforms re-encode anyway and take H.264 or HEVC happily. The strong case is **VP9 WebM with alpha**. It's the transparent-video format Chrome and Firefox play; Frame Job's HEVC-with-alpha only plays in Safari. Transparent graphics, like the ones the motion graphics engine makes, are exactly what people want to put on web pages. AV1 is mainly about smaller files for self-hosted web video, and good 10-bit HDR delivery.

My suggestion: file it as an issue now. If you want it, start with a short spike: the ffmpeg route end to end, whether AVFoundation can write AV1 into MP4, and a VP9-with-alpha WebM test against SVT-AV1/libvpx encode speeds on this machine. Then decide between the ffmpeg route and bundled encoders. Want me to file it, and should it go in Post Release?

> Is it worth it?
My brother works at Google on those codecs. I think he's disapointed that we don't support them, so yes. It is super valuable to me. Bundle the encoders.

That's settled: AV1 and VP9 export with bundled encoders. I'll record your decision in an issue, then start with a spike in its own worktree lane, running alongside the dither work. The spike measures the open questions so the road map rests on numbers.

Owner decision, 2026-10-27: Frame Job exports AV1 and VP9, with the encoders **bundled in the app**, not through a user-installed ffmpeg. "It is super valuable to me. Bundle the encoders."

## Why it needs bundling

Measured on an M2 Max, macOS 26.5.1, with `VTCopyVideoEncoderList`:
- VideoToolbox offers only these encoders: H.264, HEVC (also its alpha, depth and disparity variants), ProRes 422/4444/XQ, JPEG and H.263. There is no AV1 or VP9 encoder, and Apple's AV1 hardware on M3 and later decodes only.
- `VTIsHardwareDecodeSupported` is false for both AV1 and VP9 on this Mac.
- AVFoundation cannot write a WebM file.

Import already handles both formats: MP4 as is, WebM/Matroska through the built-in rewrap (#216, #227), and decode depends on the machine. Export does not.

## Scope, with the decisions still open

These go to a spike first, and the open choices come back to the owner:

- **AV1 encoder:** libaom (AOM's reference encoder, BSD-2 plus the AOM patent licence) or SVT-AV1 (BSD-3 plus the AOM patent licence). Measure speed and quality on Apple Silicon. rav1e (Rust) would break the "no pixel work in Rust" rule, so it needs the owner.
- **VP9 encoder:** libvpx (BSD-3), including VP9 with alpha in WebM. Chrome and Firefox play that as transparent web video; HEVC with alpha plays only in Safari.
- **Containers:**
  - AV1 in MP4: can `AVAssetWriter` write precompressed `av01` samples, or does it need a muxer of our own?
  - AV1 and VP9 in WebM: a Matroska *writer*. The core has only an index reader today.
- **Audio:** WebM carries Opus or Vorbis, not AAC, so that needs libopus (BSD-3). AV1-in-MP4 can keep AAC.
- **Depth and HDR:** 10-bit AV1, VP9 profile 2, HLG and PQ colour tags, to match the HEVC 10-bit and HDR rows.
- **Build:** each C library vendored or fetched at a pinned version, built for arm64 by the Makefile and Xcode, with provenance recorded. Their licences go in the acknowledgements (#376).
- **Speed:** software encodes run in the Export Queue. Measure 1080p30 throughput at the presets offered.
- **Product surface:** new export preset rows (spec §7.8 and §6's `export` tool, so the MCP mirror and the guide's export page), plus dist_check rows proving the libraries are in the bundle and signed.
EOF

content.text:
Two things have happened since you approved the codecs.

**AV1/VP9: the spike has started.** I filed your decision as #377 and created a separate worktree, `~/devel/framejob-codecs`. A spike is now measuring:
- **Building the encoders:** whether libaom, SVT-AV1, libvpx and libopus build as arm64 static libraries, how long that takes and how much each adds to the app. It also looks at libwebm, Google's WebM muxer.
- **Speed and quality on this Mac:** encode speed at each preset, and quality against our HEVC at the same bitrate, at 8-bit and 10-bit.
- **Containers:** whether AVFoundation can carry AV1 and VP9 in MP4, and how to write WebM.
- **Alpha:** VP9 with transparency in WebM.
- **Audio:** Opus for WebM.
- **HDR:** the colour tags AV1 and VP9 need for HLG and PQ.

When it's done I'll bring you its recommendation and the real choices: which AV1 encoder, which containers, alpha, presets and HDR. libaom and libvpx are the natural picks given your brother's work, unless the numbers argue otherwise.

**Raster dither: it works, but a default H.264 export wipes it out.** The patched tiny-skia does what it should:
- in the graphic render and in `render_frame`, the median band shrank from 19 px to 2 px;
- solid fills stayed byte-identical;
- drawing was no slower (about 9 ms per frame before and after).

But the test exports a static one-second clip, and at default quality the H.264 encoder spent only about 60 kbit/s on it. That strips out the dither noise, so the steps came back. Since an H.264 export is exactly where you saw the bands, this matters.

A correction I owe you: I told the agents that ±½ level of dither, and "colours on a level stay exact", were your constraints. They were mine. A stronger dither is open if the numbers call for it.

Before asking you to choose, I've sent the implementer to measure the cases that matter:
- the same gradient moving, as in real video;
- H.264 at 8 and 16 Mbps;
- HEVC;
- ProRes as a reference that keeps the noise.

With those numbers the choice will be between three options:
- accept the limit for low-bitrate H.264;
- raise the default export quality so gradients survive;
- use a stronger, grain-like dither.
I don't really care about low-bitrate exports. I only care about higher quality exports.

The variant measurements are in, and so far only ProRes keeps the dither.

| Export | Banding vs. no dither | What's left |
|---|---|---|
| ProRes 422 | **71 % less**; median band 19 px → 2 px | about 88 % of the dither noise survives |
| H.264 at default, 8 or 16 Mbps (still or moving) | 0–27 % less; static sometimes slightly worse | bands still 16–24 px median, 40–48 px widest |
| HEVC (8-bit) at default | 11 % less | same as H.264 |

Asking for a higher bitrate doesn't help. On smooth gradients Apple's encoder doesn't spend what it's given: the "16 Mbps" moving clip came out at about 0.6 Mbps. A ±7/16-level dither is cheap for it to throw away, and once it's gone, 8-bit H.264 has nowhere to put the in-between values, so the steps come back.

So the raster dither clearly fixes high-quality masters, but not 8-bit H.264 or HEVC at any bitrate this encoder will actually use. Before asking you, I've sent the implementer to measure two more cases:
1. **HEVC 10-bit.** I expect this to work. When the encoder smooths the dither away, the averaged values are the true in-between levels, and a 10-bit file can hold them.
2. **A stronger dither, ±1 and ±1.5 levels,** on moving H.264 at default and at 16 Mbps. It also measures how visible the noise becomes and what happens to colours that sit exactly on a level.

With those numbers the choice will probably be:
- fix it for ProRes and 10-bit exports only, which is what the dither already does;
- also add a stronger, grain-like dither so 8-bit H.264 holds up, at the cost of visible fine noise and some file size.

If 10-bit HEVC works, there's a third option: export your high-quality deliverables as HEVC 10-bit. They play everywhere modern, and YouTube accepts them.
Would a software export do a better job?
A software encoder would very likely do better. A quick test on the ProRes file the implementer already exported will tell us how much.

import subprocess, sys, struct, statistics as st
W,H=1920,1080
def frame(fn, n):
    raw=subprocess.run(["ffmpeg","-v","error","-i",fn,"-vf",f"select=eq(n\\,{n})","-frames:v","1","-f","rawvideo","-pix_fmt","rgb48le","-"],capture_output=True).stdout

for fn in sys.argv[1:]:
    raw=frame(fn, 15 if fn.endswith('.mov') else 45)
    xs=range(0,800)
    cm=[st.fmean(g(raw,x,y) for y in range(530,551)) for x in xs]   # column means, in 8-bit levels

    runs=[];c=row[0];n=0
    for v in row:

    runs.append(n)
    noise=st.fmean(abs(g(raw,x,540)-cm[x]) for x in range(32,768))

Somewhat, for 8-bit. The bigger win is 10-bit output.

I re-encoded the dithered ProRes master (3 s, the static worst case) with each encoder and measured how much stair-step remains along the gradient. Lower is smoother. A plain undithered 8-bit staircase scores about 0.29.

| Encoder | Stair-step | Dither noise left | Size (3 s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ProRes master (reference) | 0.09 | 0.22 | — |
| Apple H.264, hardware, 8 Mbps (what Frame Job uses) | **0.44** | 0.08 | 1.4 MB |
| Apple H.264, software, 8 Mbps | 0.31 | 0.41 | 1.9 MB |
| x264, CRF 18 | 0.26 | 0.53 | 236 KB |
| x264, CRF 18, `tune grain` | 0.25 | 0.59 | 88 KB |
| SVT-AV1, 8-bit | 0.30 | 0.42 | 44 KB |
| **SVT-AV1, 10-bit** | **0.11** | 0.02 | 9 KB |
| **libvpx VP9, 10-bit** | **0.11** | 0.00 | 8 KB |

What it shows:
- **Apple's hardware H.264 encoder is the worst case.** It scores worse than an undithered staircase, adding blocking on top of the steps.
- **Software 8-bit encoders do better, but not well.** x264 keeps more of the dither, but only gets to about 0.25, still far from the master. And x264 is GPL, so it can't be bundled into an Apache-2.0 app. Apple's own software H.264 encoder can be, but only gets to 0.31 and is slower.
- **10-bit encoders basically match the master.** AV1 and VP9 smooth the dither away like the others do, but a 10-bit file can hold the averaged in-between values, so the gradient comes out smooth, and in tiny files.

So for 8-bit H.264 there's no encoder setting that really fixes it: 8 bits can't hold sub-level detail through lossy compression at sensible bitrates. The real fix for high-quality deliverables is **10-bit output**: the AV1 and VP9 10-bit export you've just approved, and probably HEVC 10-bit, which already exists. The implementer is measuring HEVC 10-bit now, along with a stronger grain-like dither, in case 8-bit H.264 still matters to you.

Pixabay's own guidance says a Content ID notice is not a copyright strike and doesn't penalize your channel. Under the Pixabay license, you can usually clear the claim by disputing it with the license certificate.

- **What the notice means:** Pixabay's guide explains that a Content ID notice is informational, and the rights holder may choose to monetize, track, or block the video. A 'Content ID' notice does not mean a copyright strike or that copyrights have been infringed.
- **Dispute route:** You can dispute the claim in YouTube's form and attach the Pixabay License Certificate .txt file you downloaded. To dispute a claim via YouTube, you just have to prove that you have the rights to use the music from Pixabay. In this case, our Pixabay License Certificate file can serve as valid proof. The certificate is available from the download dropdown on the track page, for logged-in users. You can find a link to it on the pop up modal once downloaded from the Search Results page or from under the 'Download' dropdown from the Media Details page (for logged in users).
- **Contacting the creator:** Pixabay suggests messaging the track's author through their Pixabay profile, since that often speeds up the process. If that fails, Pixabay support can be contacted.
- **Why claims happen:** Some contributors register tracks with Content ID through a distributor, so a legally used track can still trigger a claim. Some contributors upload their tracks to Pixabay for free use but also register them with Content ID (directly or via a distributor). As a result, Content ID may flag your video even if you used the track legally under the Pixabay license.
- **Identifying registered tracks:** Pixabay marks Content ID-registered tracks on search results and media pages, though not every contributor flags them, so checking YouTube Creator Studio is advised.
- **Timeline:** One Pixabay guide says disputes can take up to 30 days; a German version of the same guide says up to 96 hours. The sources conflict, so treat the timeline as uncertain.
- **Don't use Report Media:** Pixabay's guide says to avoid its 'Report Media' tool for Content ID claims.

content.text:
Yes, the license allows it, and the fix is to dispute the claim with Pixabay's license certificate. YouTube most likely didn't reject the upload: it flagged it with a Content ID claim. Check which it is in YouTube Studio under the video's Copyright details.

**Why it happened.** The track page marks "Electronic Corporate" by Orvien as **"Content ID Registered"**. Some Pixabay artists give their music away for free use on Pixabay but also register it with YouTube's Content ID through a distributor. YouTube's automated matching then flags videos that use it, even legally licensed ones. Pixabay says such a claim is not a copyright strike and doesn't penalize your channel, though while it stands the claimant can monetize, track or block the video.

**Does the license cover it?** Yes. The track is "Free for use under the Pixabay Content License", which permits use in videos, including commercial and promotional ones like this. What it forbids is mainly redistributing the music on its own or as the main point of a product, which a product promo isn't.

**How to clear it**
1. **Get the license certificate.** Signed in to Pixabay, open the track page and use the **Download** dropdown. There's a link to the **Pixabay License Certificate** (a `.txt` file) for your download. It's tied to your account, so download the certificate from the same account you downloaded the track with.
2. **Dispute in YouTube Studio:** go to Content → the video → Copyright claim → **Dispute**. Choose the reason saying you have a license or permission to use the content. Give the track title, the Pixabay URL and the license, and attach the certificate or paste its text. Some guides note the form doesn't always allow an attachment; if not, paste the text or link to it.
3. **Optionally, message Orvien** through their Pixabay profile. Pixabay says that often speeds up the release.
4. **Don't** use Pixabay's "Report Media" button for this. Pixabay says it's the wrong channel for Content ID claims.

The claimant then has to release the claim or respond. Pixabay's English guide says that can take up to 30 days and its German version says up to 96 hours, so the timing is uncertain. If you'd rather not wait, I can swap the music for a track Pixabay doesn't mark "Content ID Registered" and re-export.

Sources:
- [Pixabay track page: Electronic Corporate by Orvien](https://pixabay.com/music/corporate-electronic-corporate-612068/)
- [Pixabay: How to clear a YouTube Content ID claim with a Pixabay License Certificate](https://pixabay.com/blog/posts/how-to-clear-a-youtube-content-id-claim-with-a-pix-190/)
- [Pixabay: Wie verifiziere ich die Youtube-Content-ID für Pixabay Musik?](https://pixabay.com/blog/posts/wie-verifiziere-ich-die-youtube-content-id-fur-pix-191/)
- [Pixabay FAQ](https://pixabay.com/service/faq/)

Part 1 of the dither is done and merged: **f9addd4** on main, not pushed. Graphic gradients are now dithered where tiny-skia rounds them to 8 bits.

**What it does**
- **Gradients only:** a fixed ±7/16-level pattern in tiny-skia's gradient pipeline. Flat colours, text, images and transparency are byte-identical.
- **Measured, against stock tiny-skia (lower is smoother):**

  | Output | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | Graphic render and `render_frame` (median band width) | 19 px | 2 px |
  | ProRes export (banding) | 0.32 | 0.09 |
  | HEVC 10-bit export, moving (banding) | 0.17 | 0.12 |

- **Checks:** `make gate` passes; the proof scores 9/9 on Debug and on Release, with all 9 mutants caught; the existing graphics proofs still pass.
- **Documented limit:** 8-bit H.264/HEVC exports still band, because the encoder strips the dither. The fix for gradients in a delivery file is a 10-bit export: HEVC 10-bit now, AV1/VP9 10-bit once #377 lands.

**What I fixed while integrating**
- Measurements cited from throwaway files now point at a comment on #375 that holds the full tables.
- The guide no longer claims the dither pattern itself survives HEVC 10-bit. It says what actually happens: the encoder smooths the pattern away, but 10 bits keep the in-between shades.
- `CLAUDE.md` gained the `graphic/vendor/` map entry and the vendoring rules, including why both crates need the patch table.
- The README's licence section now names tiny-skia's BSD-3-Clause licence.

**Part 2, the output dither, needs a decision from you.** It was aimed mainly at 8-bit H.264, which we now know strips it. What's left for it to help is the compositor's own float gradients (fades, dissolves, grading, deep video) when they're written as:
- 8-bit stills: `render_frame` and Save Frame as PNG or JPEG;
- GIF and APNG.

It wouldn't help any video export you care about: ProRes and 10-bit already keep those values. My recommendation is to drop part 2 and close #375, leaving a short note in the spec.        | Balanced (default) | 6 | about 75 fps | 44–52 % |
       | Smaller file | 4 | about 41 fps | 52–58 % |

I fed it packets straight from aomenc and vpxenc, with the `av1C` and `vpcC` records built by our own code and an AAC track beside them. Every frame decoded identical to the encoder's output. HLG and PQ colour tags and the HDR10 mastering metadata were written too.
       - Libaom puts a temporal-delimiter unit in every packet. The AV1-in-MP4 spec says these should not be stored, so they need stripping.
       - `AVAssetWriter` leaves the `av01` brand out of the file header, which the AV1-in-MP4 spec requires. A 4-byte patch after writing fixes it.

  4. **Alpha.** VP9 alpha in WebM works both through ffmpeg and through two libvpx streams muxed by libwebm. The decoded alpha matches the source to a mean error of 0.02 code values.
     - **Browsers:** Chrome supports it since Chrome 31, and Firefox has a WebM alpha test fixed for Firefox 53. That Safari drops the alpha comes only from secondary sources, so it needs a person to check.
     - **AV1 alpha** does not exist in practice: neither encoder can take an alpha channel.

  - **AV1 on older Macs:** M1/M2 cannot decode AV1.

  - **Build:** cmake must be on the publish runner.

  - **C1:** AV1 in MP4, 8-bit.
  - **C2:** 10-bit AV1 and HDR.
  - **C3:** WebM writer and Opus.
  - **C4:** VP9 in WebM.
  - **C5:** VP9 alpha.

  7. **HDR on the new rows:** AV1 10-bit with HLG/PQ (recommended); VP9 Profile 2 HDR later, WebM only.
  8. **Sources:** fetch pinned tarballs checked by SHA-256 and cache them (recommended), or vendor them in the repo.

  `-RCCodecProbe 1`. The gate, the probe builder, the tree copies, the four spikes' own build
  lines and the publish workflow's cmake. **Acceptance:** `make gate` passes; `dist_check`
  41/41 with a stand-in Sparkle key (D36–D41: the encoder symbols in both executables, no load

  existing cancel flag checked per frame by the pump and the queue, and the flush before

content.text:
C1's design (AV1 in MP4, 8-bit) is done and is now in adversarial review. It needed no decision from you.

**What you'll see:**
- **A new export format,** "AV1 (MP4)", listed after HEVC 10-bit. It has AAC sound and works over MCP as well (`export {preset: "av1"}`).
- **A Speed popup under Format** with Faster, Balanced (the default) and Smaller file. It's greyed out for other formats, the way Quality already is, and remembers your last choice. Over MCP it's `encoder_speed: faster | balanced | smaller`.
- **A keyframe at least every 2 seconds,** so the file scrubs and seeks well.

**Under the hood:**
- **In the Rust core:** the core parses the encoder's output to build the AV1 header the MP4 needs. It also strips the per-frame markers that don't belong in MP4 and adds the `av01` brand AVFoundation leaves out. If it can't add the brand, the export fails rather than writing a non-conforming file.
- **In Swift:** each frame is converted to the encoder's pixel format on the GPU and fed to SVT-AV1 on its own queue, with progress and cancel. SVT-AV1's log output goes through Frame Job's logging instead of stderr.
- **Clean-ups first:** three files at the size cap give up code in pure moves before C1 adds anything.

**Proof:** a new AV1 export proof checks every frame decodes, using ffmpeg's AV1 decoder since this Mac has no hardware one. It also checks that sound lines up, that cancel leaves no file, and the rate on your real `IMG_0018.MOV`, plus 8 mutants. Playback on an M3 or later becomes a manual check for you (SE-17).

The review will test three judgement calls:
- how the row tells AVFoundation to write the container;
- finishing the encoder's last frames on cancel (up to about a second) rather than stopping it instantly;
- a GPU scaler doing the resizing that AVFoundation does for the other formats.

The `av1` pump cannot tell a failed read from a finished one, so a read that fails partway gives a truncated file branded and reported as `done`. Fix: pass a read-failure closure into `run` and call `fail` with it when a sample comes back nil.
  2. **The `all-sync` mutant survives A5.** If every sample is marked sync, the first packet is K and the largest K-to-K gap is one frame, so A5 still passes. It is 01-spec.md with the changes below, plus the "Objections addressed" section at the end. I accepted all five objections: each had evidence, and I confirmed objection 1 by reading `ExporterWriter.swift:400-419` in the worktree. I added no other scope.
  
  Changes:
  1. **Read failure:** `ExportEncodePump.run` takes a new closure, `readFailure: @escaping () -> (any Error)?`. It returns nil unless the reader's status is failed, and then returns the reader's error, falling back to the existing pump's message "The composition could not be read to the end." When the reader returns no sample, the pump checks this first. A failed read now fails the export and takes the stop path, so it no longer sends end-of-stream, finishes and brands a truncated file. Step 7 passes the closure in from `start`.
  2. **Stop path (step 6):** `markAsFinished` and `group.leave()` run exactly once, in a `defer` with a once-flag, on every exit. If the encoder throws (`send`, `sendEndOfStream` or `nextPacket`), the export fails, end-of-stream and the drain are skipped, and the encoder is left for `close()`. `nextPacket(wait: true)` is never called after a throw. A plain cancel still sends end-of-stream and drains, discarding the packets.
  3. **A3 split in two:**
     - A3a checks the sequence header's `color_config` through `trace_headers`: the colour-description flag is 1, primaries, transfer and matrix are 1/1/1, and the range is 0.
     - A3b reads the `colr` box from the MP4's bytes and checks it is `nclx` 1/1/1 with full_range 0.
  
     The `colour-untagged` mutant is split the same way: `colour-untagged-bitstream` is caught by A3a and `colour-untagged-container` by A3b.
  4. **A5 tightened:** it runs on A1's 5 s file. The number of key packets must be at most ceil(duration / 2 s) + 1, and there must be at least one non-key packet. Through `trace_headers`, every packet flagged as key must be a KEY_FRAME, and no unflagged packet may be one.

Under the current model (AV1 gets HEVC's bitrate, its efficiency going into quality), that undershoot hands back a third of the quality gain. How should AV1's rate work?

options.label: Capped constant quality (Recommended)
options.description: AV1 encodes to a constant quality (CRF) chosen to match or beat HEVC, with the requested bitrate as a ceiling. Quality is steady and as good as asked, and simple scenes come out smaller. File size isn't fixed in advance.

options.label: Scale the target
options.description: Keep VBR but aim higher (about ×1.5) so the file lands near the requested rate. Predictable sizes, but it's a correction factor measured on one clip and content-dependent.

options.label: Accept as is
options.description: Leave VBR at the requested rate and record the ~33 % undershoot. Files are smaller than asked, with quality still about level with HEVC.

questions.question: Capped constant quality hit a trade-off. With a strict cap (files never over the requested bitrate), SVT-AV1 starves some frames, so on your IMG_0018 clip the Faster speed lands about 0.1–0.4 VMAF below HEVC. That's well under what anyone can see (about 1–2 VMAF), but it's below the 'match or beat HEVC' bar. With SVT's default looser cap, quality beats HEVC on every clip measured, but a hard clip can run up to about 1.2× the requested rate. Typical files still come in well under it: your clip at 0.65–0.74 of the cap. Which matters more?

input.prompt: Handoff dir: /Users/kevingalligan/.claude/litecode/framejob/codecs-c2/. Templates dir: /Users/kevingalligan/.claude-personal/skills/litecode/references/. Read 01-spec.md and only the files it names. Write 02-objections.md.

content.text:
C2's design is done and is now in adversarial review. It settled the row question from your earlier choices, so it didn't need you: **AV1 will always be 10-bit**, in the one `av1` row. There will be no separate `av1_10bit` row.

The reasons:
- you chose exactly four rows;
- the existing decision already says the AV1 rows are 10-bit;
- unlike HEVC, AV1's standard profile decodes 8- and 10-bit alike, so an 8-bit-only AV1 row protects no player;
- it fits your "higher quality" priority.

The cost is real but modest. The spike measured Balanced dropping from 75 to 64 fps and memory rising from 1.15 to 1.61 GB at 1080p. It's recorded as an accepted risk in the new decision, CX-14.

**HDR on the AV1 row:**
- In an HDR project, the Dynamic Range choice (HLG, HDR10 or SDR version) works on AV1 the same way it does on HEVC 10-bit.
- The colour tags go both in the AV1 stream and in the MP4.
- HDR10 exports carry the mastering and light-level metadata in both places.

**Quality bar:** AV1's quality is now compared against HEVC 10-bit instead of 8-bit HEVC. All 15 quality-level settings are re-checked on your clip, and any that fall short are lowered until they match or beat HEVC 10-bit.

**One gap fixed:** the HDR guide page didn't list AV1 among the formats that write the SDR version. C2 fixes that.

**Owed to you:** a new manual check, HDR-8, for HDR AV1 playback on an M3 or later.

content.text:
The adversarial review of C2's design found three problems in its tests. None of them changes how C2 works, and the design is being revised now:

1. **One mutant was expected to fail the wrong set of checks.** Removing AV1 from the HDR rows breaks three more checks than the design listed. Under the proof's "exactly these rows" rule, that run would have counted as a failure even though the mutant was caught.
2. **The HDR10-metadata test couldn't see its own mutant.** When an AV1 stream carries no HDR10 metadata, this Mac's ffmpeg fills it in from the MP4 box. So stripping the metadata from the stream would have gone unnoticed. The fix reads the stream on its own, with no container.
3. **One quality setting was never re-checked at 10 bits.** Faster at Medium quality was calibrated on a different clip, by hundredths of a VMAF point. It gets its own 10-bit re-check.

I've also asked for one risk the review couldn't prove to be fixed in the design itself. The colour-accuracy check averaged over the whole picture, which could hide a wrong colour matrix that only shows in saturated colours. It now also scores a saturated-colour patch.
